name: Pandan
tagline: The green, sweet smell of Nyonya kaya and kueh.
story: Pandan is the defining aroma of Malay and Peranakan sweets: kueh, green Nyonya kaya, and the leaves wrapped around Nyonya rice dumplings.
When fruit for jam was hard to find, Hainanese and Peranakan cooks made kaya from coconut milk, eggs and pandan leaves instead. That's the kaya on your toast today.

sources.title: BiblioAsia: The Evolution of Chinese Food in Singapore

everyday.text: Pandan chiffon cake is the green, cloud-light cake of every Singapore bakery. The earliest local newspaper mention is a 1972 review of Bali Café.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Pandan

everyday.text: Pandan chicken is marinated chicken wrapped in the leaves and fried, so the smell cooks right into it.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Pandan

everyday.text: Many Singaporeans tuck fresh pandan leaves into cars and cupboards to keep cockroaches away. Pest experts say fresh leaves only mildly repel them, and dried ones can turn into food.

src.title: Rentokil Singapore: is pandan a cockroach repellent?

name: Jasmine
tagline: The flower of Little India's garland stalls.
story: Jasmine is one of the main fragrant flowers in Hindu garland-making, alongside rose, tuberose and chrysanthemum.
Garland makers have worked Little India's five-foot-ways for decades. Jothi Store & Flower Shop began in the early 1960s as a small stall selling garlands, betel leaves and prayer items.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Making of Flower Garlands
NHB Roots: Jothi Store & Flower Shop

everyday.text: At Tamil Hindu weddings, the couple exchange garlands as a sign of union and mutual trust.

src.title: NHB Roots: Making of Flower Garlands

everyday.text: Garlands come out for Pongal and Deepavali, for Thaipusam processions, and to bless a new home, car or shop.

src.title: NHB Roots: Making of Flower Garlands

everyday.text: Across South India and its diaspora, women string jasmine into their hair for festivals and offer it to the gods.

src.title: Deccan Herald: The many lives of the jasmine

lore.text: Prayer flowers are never just thrown away: unsold puja garlands are returned to nature, at the foot of a tree or in compost.

src.title: NHB Roots: Making of Flower Garlands

name: Nutmeg & mace
tagline: The spice that named Orchard Road.
story: One tree gives two spices: nutmeg is the seed, and mace is the red, lacy covering around it.

Raffles sent nutmeg seeds and saplings from Bencoolen in Sumatra. In the 1830s and 1840s, European residents turned old gambier estates around Orchard Road into nutmeg orchards, which are believed to have given the road its name. A disease wiped out the trees in 1857.

everyday.text: Nutmeg trees still grow in the Singapore Botanic Gardens, some of them listed on NParks' Heritage Tree Register.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Nutmeg

everyday.text: In traditional remedies, nutmeg has been used for rheumatism and an upset stomach.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Nutmeg

name: Clove
tagline: Raffles' bet on the spice trade.
story: In 1822, Raffles set up Singapore's first botanical and experimental garden on Fort Canning Hill to grow cash crops, mainly nutmeg and clove.
At one point it held over 600 nutmeg trees and 300 clove plants. The garden closed in 1829, but a replica Spice Garden grows on the same slopes today.

sources.title: NParks: Fort Canning Park special features

everyday.text: Biting on a clove is an old toothache remedy. Its oil, mostly eugenol, numbs pain, which is why clove still turns up in toothpaste.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Clove

everyday.text: Cloves were also used to freshen linens and clothes, and next door in Indonesia they scent kretek cigarettes.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Clove

everyday.text: NParks runs free guided tours of the Fort Canning Spice Garden, where you can smell clove and nutmeg on the tree.

src.title: NParks: Spice Garden tour

name: Black pepper (& gambier)
tagline: Singapore's first plantation crop.
story: Gambier and pepper were grown together, mostly by Teochew planters, and were already on the island when the British arrived in 1819.

By the late 1840s there were some 400 to 600 gambier and pepper plantations, and they drove large-scale clearing of Singapore's forests. Gambier itself was used for tanning, not perfume. Pepper is the note that carries the story.

everyday.text: Pepper is the soul of Teochew bak kut teh: a clear pork-rib soup seasoned only with garlic, soy sauce and pepper.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Bak kut teh

everyday.text: Kai Juan Bak Kut Teh on the Balestier food trail has served the clear, peppery Teochew style for about 50 years.

src.title: NHB Roots: Kai Juan Bak Kut Teh

name: Orchid
tagline: A hybrid national flower for a hybrid nation.
story: Agnes Joaquim, an Armenian Singaporean, bred the Vanda Miss Joaquim in her Tanjong Pagar garden, and it was described in 1893. It became Singapore's national flower on 15 April 1981. Singapore is the only country with a hybrid as its national flower.
Most orchids are only faintly scented, so an orchid note in perfume is an accord: an impression the perfumer builds from other materials.

everyday.text: Orchid diplomacy: since 1956, Singapore has named orchid hybrids after visiting leaders and guests. The first was Aranthera Anne Black; there are now more than 280.

src.title: MFA: Orchid book launch (2024)

everyday.text: The VIP orchids grow in the VIP Orchid Garden at the National Orchid Garden, inside the Botanic Gardens.

src.title: BiblioAsia: Singapore's Orchid Diplomacy

everyday.text: Orchids are the garland flower for secular events, chosen for their colour and their almost neutral scent.

src.title: NHB Roots: Making of Flower Garlands

name: Agarwood (oud) & sandalwood
local: gaharu · cendana · 沉香 · 檀香
tagline: The woods of mosque, temple and shophouse.
story: Malay and Muslim: minyak attar, an alcohol-free perfume oil, is listed as Singapore intangible cultural heritage, and agarwood is a key ingredient. Kampong Gelam became the trade's centre because of Sultan Mosque, where worshippers put on attar before prayers.
Chinese: joss-stick burning spread with 19th-century Chinese migration. Temple incense is often made with sandalwood or agarwood.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Making of Joss Sticks

everyday.text: Muslims in Singapore still burn agarwood chips as incense at religious gatherings, such as Ramadan prayers in the lead-up to Hari Raya Haji.

src.title: NHB Roots: Minyak Attar

everyday.text: During the seventh lunar month, joss sticks, paper offerings and food appear along pavements and void decks to feed wandering spirits.

src.title: NHB Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)

lore.text: The Hungry Ghost Festival rests on the belief that spirits without descendants to make offerings to them go hungry, so believers burn incense and paper for them.

src.title: NHB Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)

name: Aquatic ginger
tagline: A beach-and-swamp ginger brought back from the brink.
story: A native ginger of sandy beaches and swamp forests, with small white to pale pink flowers. It's Critically Endangered in Singapore; in the wild it's recorded on Pulau Semakau.

NParks has salvaged it and replanted it along some Nature Ways, the planted streets that link up green spaces. You can see it at HortPark, Kent Ridge Park and the Botanic Gardens' Ginger Garden. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Alpinia aquatica

everyday.text: Crush a leaf and it smells: the whole plant holds aromatic oils.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Alpinia aquatica

everyday.text: Its leaves feed the caterpillars of the Chocolate Demon butterfly, and birds eat its small black berries.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Alpinia aquatica

name: Common dianella
tagline: Looks like wild grass, until the blue berries show up.
story: A tough native herb with sword-shaped leaves (that's what ensifolia means). It grows from Labrador Park's rocky shore to Chek Jawa, Kent Ridge and St John's Island.

Its flowers are tiny, white to bluish, and open in the afternoon. Then come shiny deep-blue berries, which birds eat; they're thought to be toxic to people. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dianella ensifolia
NParks Buzz: 10 Native Plants of Singapore

everyday.text: NParks' own gardeners say it may be why people think native plants are just 'wild grass'.

src.title: NParks Buzz: 10 Native Plants of Singapore

everyday.text: In the region its roots have gone into cosmetics and perfume, and its boiled leaves into incense.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dianella ensifolia

lore.text: The genus is named after Diana, the Roman goddess of the wild.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dianella ensifolia

name: Seashore purslane
tagline: A salty succulent that creeps along the shore.
story: A creeping succulent with fleshy leaves that grows on salty, sandy and muddy ground by the sea. In Malay it's gelang laut or gelang pasir.

In Singapore you'll find it on Pulau Ubin, Pulau Tekong, Pulau Semakau and at the end of Lim Chu Kang Road. Its small star-shaped flowers are green outside and pink inside. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Sesuvium portulacastrum

everyday.text: Around the world it's eaten as a sea vegetable, raw, pickled or cooked.

src.title: Frontiers in Plant Science (2024)

name: Simpoh lak
tagline: Big yellow flowers that last a single day.
story: A riverside tree up to about 25 m tall, with bright yellow flowers 8 to 10 cm across around a dark red centre. Each flower opens early in the morning and drops its petals by evening.
One honest note: Singapore Airlines calls all six batik flowers native, but NParks lists simpoh lak as non-native to Singapore. Its home range is Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dillenia excelsa

everyday.text: The flowers are full of nectar and mostly worked by giant honey bees.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dillenia excelsa

everyday.text: Another native, the simpoh air, has leaves so big that hawkers once wrapped tempeh and rojak in them, before plastic bags took over.

src.title: NParks: Simpoh Air

lore.text: Its cut branches root so easily that fences built from them have sprouted back into trees.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dillenia excelsa

name: Utania nervosa
tagline: A rare tree botanists mislabelled for half a century.
story: A small native tree, usually 1 to 5 m tall, with hanging clusters of cream-yellow to white flowers. It's listed as Vulnerable in Singapore and has no common English name.
In 1962 it was misidentified as Fagraea racemosa. It wasn't sorted out until a 2014 revision of the genus. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Utania nervosa

everyday.text: It belongs to the same plant family as the tembusu, the tree on the back of the $5 note.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Cyrtophyllum fragrans (Tembusu)

name: White kopsia
tagline: Red and white, like the flag.
story: White petals around a red throat: the colours of Singapore's flag. It was named Kopsia singapurensis in 1923, decades before the flag existed. Its five petals are fused at the base, which NParks jokes makes them 'united'.

It's fragrant, each flower lasts a day, and in the wild here it grows only in Nee Soon Swamp Forest. It's Critically Endangered in Singapore and found nowhere else but Peninsular Malaysia. One of the six batik-motif flowers in Singapore Airlines' Batik Flora.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Kopsia singapurensis
NParks: Six native plants named after Singapore

lore.text: In 1964 a kopsia was used in place of a ribbon to open the rebuilt herbarium at the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Kopsia singapurensis

name: Kopi & teh
tagline: The smell of a Nanyang breakfast.
story: Between the 1920s and 1950s, Hainanese coffeeshop owners popularised kopitiam culture and the Nanyang breakfast: kopi, teh, soft-boiled eggs and kaya toast. Teh is usually made with Ceylon tea.
Nanyang means 'South Sea' in Mandarin and refers to Southeast Asia. Nanyang-style kopi is traditionally made from Robusta beans roasted with sugar and margarine, then strained through a cloth 'sock'.

sources.title: NHB Roots: Traditional Breakfast of Kaya and Kopi

everyday.text: Kopitiam code: kopi comes with condensed milk, O means no milk, C means evaporated milk, kosong means no sugar, siew dai less sugar, peng iced.

src.title: Honeycombers: how to order kopi

everyday.text: Teh tarik, pulled tea, was first sold by Indian-Muslim drink stalls after World War II. It is poured back and forth between two cups until it froths, ideally further than arm's length.

src.title: NHB: Teh tarik photo story

everyday.text: It's also called a mamak drink, from the Tamil word for uncle.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Teh tarik

name: Calamansi
tagline: The small lime on every hawker plate.
story: Calamansi, called limau kasturi in Malay, is the small lime squeezed over dishes at Singapore's hawker centres, from Hokkien mee to Malay noodles and sambal belacan.
The plant first came from the Philippines, where it is still mostly grown. NParks lists it under both names, along with 'musk lime' and 'golden lime'.

everyday.text: Fried Hokkien prawn noodles always come with sambal and a calamansi lime on the side. You squeeze it yourself.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Fried Hokkien prawn noodles

everyday.text: In December 2020, Singapore's hawker culture became its first entry on UNESCO's list of Intangible Cultural Heritage.

src.title: AFAR: UNESCO adds Singapore's hawker culture

everyday.text: Citrus plants like kumquat and four-season lime crowd doorways at Chinese New Year. Kumquat's Cantonese name, gam gat, sounds like 'gold and luck'.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Kumquat

name: Frangipani
tagline: The graveyard flower, and a perfumer's name.
story: NParks lists the white frangipani as the 'Singapore graveyard flower'. Its Malay names include kemboja and bunga kubur, 'grave flower'. Indian and Malay Muslims and Buddhists often plant it in cemeteries. Some Malay Muslims see its fallen morning flowers as an offering to the dead, and Hindus sometimes plant it near temples.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Plumeria obtusa

lore.text: In Malay folklore, the pontianak, the ghost of a woman who died in childbirth, gives off a strong smell of frangipani when she is near.

src.title: Wikipedia: Ghosts in Malay culture

lore.text: The flower was named after a perfume: a 17th-century almond glove scent made by the Marquis Muzio Frangipani. Its smell reminded botanists of his perfume.

src.title: JSTOR Daily: Plant of the month, frangipani

name: Torch ginger
tagline: The pink bud that perfumes rojak and laksa.
story: Torch ginger, bunga kantan, is grown for its aromatic young flower buds, which taste floral and tangy. NParks calls them a key ingredient in Chinese rojak and Penang asam laksa.
It grows in the Fort Canning Spice Garden today, next to the nutmeg and clove.

sources.title: NParks: Three Essential Herbs and Spices in Local Dishes
NParks: Ancient History Trail at Fort Canning

name: Bandung
tagline: Pink rose syrup and milk, over a lot of ice.
story: Rose cordial stirred into evaporated or condensed milk, which turns it bright pink. It's a drinks-stall staple in Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei.
It's usually traced to the rose milk served in India, made here with evaporated milk.

everyday.text: TIME magazine once described it as looking exactly like a cold glass of Pepto-Bismol.

src.title: TIME: Air bandung

name: Durian
tagline: The smell that got banned from the MRT.
story: Singapore's favourite fruit and its most argued-about smell. In 1988 the MRT Corporation banned durians from trains because the smell lingers long after the fruit is gone, and air-conditioning makes it worse. The crossed-out durian sign is still up on trains and buses.
A wild species, Durio singaporensis, is named after Singapore.

everyday.text: Durians are mostly eaten at roadside stalls. Singapore's first durian restaurant opened in Hougang in 1983.

src.title: Remember Singapore: roadside durian stalls

lore.text: An old saying sums it up: the flavour of heaven and the smell of hell.

src.title: Remember Singapore: roadside durian stalls

name: Kaya
tagline: Coconut, egg and pandan, spread on toast.
story: Kaya is coconut cream, eggs, sugar and pandan cooked slowly into a thick custard jam. It's eaten on toast with cold butter, next to kopi and soft-boiled eggs.

Nobody agrees where it started. Some say it's a Eurasian take on a Portuguese egg jam, some credit Hainanese cooks, and a 1920s coffee-shop worker recalled it as Malay food that Hainanese coffee shops adapted.

everyday.text: Kheng Hoe Heng, opened in 1919, is the oldest Hainanese coffee shop in Singapore; Ya Kun has been toasting since 1944.

src.title: Visit Singapore: Kaya toast

everyday.text: At Chin Mee Chin in Katong, the kaya was cooked over slow-burning charcoal.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Chin Mee Chin Confectionery

name: Gula melaka
tagline: Smoky dark sugar from a coconut palm's flower.
story: Gula melaka is made from the sap of the coconut palm's flower bud. Tappers cut slits in the bud, tie a pot underneath, then boil the sap down into dark, caramel-like blocks. It's named after Melaka.
It's the dark syrup in chendol, the molten centre of ondeh-ondeh, and the pour over sago pudding.

everyday.text: The nipah palm of the mangroves is tapped for sugar too, and its sap also goes into gula melaka.

src.title: NParks Buzz: Eat straight from your palm

name: Chempaka
tagline: The temple flower perfumers prize.
story: Magnolia champaca is a tall tree with fragrant pale-yellow flowers that deepen to orange, blooming through the year here. The flowers are rich in essential oil, used for perfume and hair oil.
Its white cousin, Magnolia × alba, is the cempaka putih, or white chempaka.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Magnolia champaca
NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Magnolia × alba

everyday.text: The flowers are used as offerings at Hindu and Buddhist temples.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Magnolia champaca

lore.text: Names overlap: NParks also lists cempaka among the Malay names for frangipani.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Plumeria obtusa

name: Tembusu
tagline: The $5-note tree that smells sweetest at night.
story: A native tree up to 30 m tall with deeply grooved bark. Its cream flowers turn yellow, are fragrant at night, and are followed by red berries that bats and birds eat.
The tree on the back of the Singapore $5 note is a real one: it stands on Lawn E in the Singapore Botanic Gardens.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Cyrtophyllum fragrans

everyday.text: Eight tembusu are listed as Heritage Trees around Singapore.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Cyrtophyllum fragrans

name: Joss sticks
tagline: The smoke of the seventh month.
story: Joss sticks burn at Chinese temples and home altars all year, but most of all in the seventh lunar month, Zhong Yuan Jie, when offerings are made to wandering spirits.
During the month, temples hold prayers and burn offerings, and estates fill with the smell of incense and joss paper.

sources.title: Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)
Ang Mo Kio Town Council: Burning joss paper

everyday.text: Town councils put out metal burning bins in the seventh month and ask residents not to burn incense or joss paper on grass, walkways or near cars.

src.title: Ang Mo Kio Town Council: Burning joss paper

lore.text: The spirits are called hungry because they have no descendants left to make offerings to them.

src.title: Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)

name: Bunga rampai
tagline: Shredded pandan and flowers, handed out at weddings.
story: Bunga rampai is finely cut pandan leaves mixed with flowers scented with rosewater or orange blossom water. Guests at a Malay wedding are given some to mark the occasion.
The pandan in it is the same leaf that flavours kaya and kueh; its fragrance has long been used in potpourri for ceremonies.

everyday.text: Community clubs run bunga rampai workshops where you shred the pandan and blend in flowers and oils yourself.

src.title: onePA: Bunga rampai workshop

name: Tiger Balm
tagline: Camphor and menthol in a little hexagonal jar.
story: Tiger Balm began as an ointment made by Aw Chu Kin, a Chinese herbalist in Rangoon. After he died in 1908, his sons Aw Boon Haw ('gentle tiger') and Aw Boon Par ('gentle leopard') refined it. Boon Haw moved to Singapore in 1926 and built a much bigger factory here.
Its smell is mostly camphor and menthol, with clove and cajuput oils. In Singapore, the red and white balms are 25% camphor.

sources.title: South China Morning Post: The Tiger Balm story

everyday.text: Haw Par Villa, the park of painted statues on Pasir Panjang Road, opened in 1937 as Tiger Balm Gardens.

src.title: Time Out Singapore: Tiger Balm

name: Ylang-ylang
tagline: The perfume tree with curly yellow petals.
story: In Malay it's kenanga, a tree with drooping, curly yellow-green flowers. NParks lists it as the 'perfume tree': the genus name comes from a Tagalog word and refers to the perfume made from its flowers.
Malaysians and Indonesians are very fond of the scent, and women traditionally tuck a flower in their hair.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Cananga odorata

everyday.text: Its flowers are also used to decorate festivities and celebrations across the region.

src.title: PROSEA: Cananga odorata

name: Tuberose
tagline: The night flower with a ghostly Malay name.
story: Tuberose blooms white and strongest at night. In Malay it's sundal malam; in Indonesian it's sedap malam, 'pleasant at night'. NParks lists it as a popular cut flower.

Its name carries a ghost story: the 2004 Malaysian horror film Pontianak Harum Sundal Malam tied it to the pontianak. Folklore enthusiasts point out the 'sundal' tree of the old tales may be a different plant.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Agave amica 'The Pearl'
Tutu Dutta: In search of the sundal tree

lore.text: In Malay folklore, the night-scented 'sundal' is said to attract spirits, which is how a perfume flower ended up in a horror title.

src.title: Tutu Dutta: In search of the sundal tree

name: Mandarin orange
tagline: Two in each hand: gold for the New Year.
story: At Chinese New Year you visit with a pair of mandarin oranges and hand them to the host, who gives a pair back. In Cantonese the fruit, gam, sounds like the word for gold.
In Malay it's limau langkat or limau kupas. Oil from the peel goes into perfume and cologne.

everyday.text: Pairs are given because even numbers are lucky; the oranges are passed with both hands.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Chinese New Year

lore.text: On chap goh mei, the 15th night, single women in Singapore throw oranges into the Singapore River, wishing for a husband.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Chinese New Year

name: Vetiver
tagline: The 'fragrant root' woven into mats.
story: Vetiver is a tall grass whose long white roots smell earthy and woody when crushed. In Malay it's akar wangi, 'fragrant root'; in India it's khus.
NParks notes its root oil is in a huge share of Western perfumes, including Chanel No. 5.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Chrysopogon zizanioides

everyday.text: Its roots are woven into mats, fans and screens that smell stronger when they're damp. In India, wet vetiver screens cool rooms in the heat.

src.title: PROSEA: Vetiveria zizanioides

name: Ginger
tagline: The bite in a cup of teh halia.
story: In Malay ginger is halia, and teh halia is milk tea made with fresh ginger juice and condensed milk, pulled like teh tarik. It's a standard order at Indian Muslim drink stalls.
Teh tarik itself traces back to Indian Muslim sarabat stalls that served rubber plantation workers after the Second World War.

sources.title: Roots: Making and sharing of tea

everyday.text: Bhai Sarbat in Kampong Gelam took its name from teh sarabat, its ginger milk tea.

src.title: Roots: Bhai Sarbat

name: Lotus
tagline: Rises clean out of the mud.
story: The lotus symbolises purity in Buddhism and divinity in Hinduism, because it blooms above the water without touching the mud. It's offered at temples, especially around Vesak Day.
Its seeds become lotus seed paste, the classic filling in mooncakes for the Mid-Autumn Festival.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Nelumbo nucifera
Gardens by the Bay: Nelumbo nucifera

everyday.text: Its big leaves wrap glutinous rice for steaming, which gives the rice a soft, grassy smell.

src.title: Gardens by the Bay: Nelumbo nucifera

name: Lemongrass
tagline: The grass that named Geylang Serai.
story: Serai is Malay for lemongrass, a clumping grass with a sharp lemony smell. It used to be farmed in the area now called Geylang Serai.
Bruised stalks go into rendang, curries, asam pedas and laksa paste; a whole stalk is often dropped into the pot as it cooks.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Cymbopogon citratus

everyday.text: Its cousin serai wangi, citronella grass, smells far stronger and is the one used to keep mosquitoes away.

src.title: BIDARA: Cymbopogon nardus

name: Limau purut
tagline: The bumpy lime with double leaves.
story: Limau purut means 'rough-skinned lime' in Malay, after its knobbly fruit. The leaves are what most kitchens use, added to curries and tom yum for a sharp lemon smell.
Many cooks now avoid its old English name, which carries a slur; makrut lime is the more neutral one.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Citrus hystrix

everyday.text: The fruit has very little juice, sour and a bit bitter; it's the rind and leaves that carry the smell.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Citrus hystrix

lore.text: Across the region the fruit's juice has long been used as a hair wash.

src.title: UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection: Kaffir lime

name: Attar
tagline: Alcohol-free perfume oil, sold by the mosque.
story: Attar, or minyak attar, is perfume oil with no alcohol, drawn from flowers, herbs and spices. In Kampong Gelam it's been sold since 1933, when Tamil Muslim trader Hanifa Kazura opened a shop that his son Jamal turned into Jamal Kazura Aromatics in the mid-1970s.
It's now known as Singapore's oldest homegrown perfume business, with branches on North Bridge Road and Bussorah Street. Grandson Johari runs Sifr Aromatics on Arab Street.

sources.title: New Straits Times: The streets of Kampung Glam

everyday.text: Johari Kazura says that if you went to a mosque, there was a good chance you'd find free perfume inside or perfume shops around it, because God likes good smells at prayer.

src.title: Roots: Sifr Aromatics

name: Haze
tagline: The burning smell that blows in from Sumatra.
story: In the dry months, smoke from land and forest fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan drifts across the Straits. On 24 September 2015 the PSI crossed 300 into the hazardous range, and schools closed the next day.
People often notice a burnt smell before the numbers rise. NEA has explained that the smell can come from compounds the PSI doesn't measure.

sources.title: NASA: Hazardous air quality in Singapore (2015)
Asia News Network: Southeast Asia's worst haze episodes
Wild Singapore News: PSI hits highest in 2 years

everyday.text: Haze season usually runs from about May to October, when winds carry the smoke over from Sumatra.

src.title: The Jakarta Post: Expect haze in Singapore

name: Marigold
tagline: Orange garlands strung along Campbell Lane.
story: Garland makers in Little India string marigold, jasmine and rose into offerings for the temples on Serangoon Road. For Hindus, saffron orange is a sacred colour and yellow signifies sanctity.
Garland-making came with the Indian diaspora and is listed in Singapore's intangible cultural heritage inventory.

sources.title: Gardens by the Bay: Mexican marigold

everyday.text: Kavadi bearers sometimes wear garlands in the Thaipusam procession, and at a Tamil Hindu wedding the couple exchange garlands.

src.title: Roots: Making of flower garlands

name: Pomelo leaves
tagline: A citrus bath to wash off the old year.
story: On the eve of Chinese New Year, some families boil pomelo leaves and bathe in the green water to wash away the past year's bad luck. The same leaves are used after funerals and before moving into a new home.
The fruit itself sits on New Year tables for luck.

sources.title: USC Folklore Archives: Bath of pomelo leaves

lore.text: Pomelo leaves are believed to clean away 'dirty, evil stuff', so they're also tied to brooms for the pre-New Year spring clean.

src.title: USC Folklore Archives: Bath of pomelo leaves

name: Rose
tagline: In the garland, the syrup and the wedding potpourri.
story: Rose turns up all over Singapore. It's one of the three classic garland flowers in Little India, with marigold and jasmine. Rose syrup makes bandung pink.
Rosewater scents the flowers in bunga rampai, the potpourri guests take home from Malay weddings.

name: Betel leaf
tagline: The leaf offered to say yes.
story: Chewing sireh, betel leaf wrapped around lime paste and shaved areca nut, was once a social necessity in Malay, Indian and Peranakan homes. Offering someone a leaf was an invitation, a friendly gesture or a sign of agreement.
Peranakan nonyas kept it in a tempat sireh, a box of small containers for the leaf, gambier, lime and sliced nut. The habit has since fallen out of fashion.

everyday.text: At Malay weddings the tepak sireh, a betel set covered in gold-embroidered velvet, leads the procession of gifts at the proposal and engagement.

src.title: Jurnal Pengajian Melayu: Tepak sirih in Malay wedding customs

name: Star anise
tagline: The licorice note in a pot of bak kut teh.
story: Bak kut teh, Hokkien for 'meat bone tea', is pork ribs stewed with garlic, cloves, cinnamon, star anise, fennel seeds and coriander. Singapore has three traditional styles: Hokkien, Teochew and Cantonese.
The Teochew style, now the most common here, is clear and peppery and skips most of the spices. The dark, herbal Hokkien style is where the star anise comes through.

sources.title: Johor Kaki: History of Singapore bak kut teh

lore.text: A popular legend says coolies on the Singapore River made the first pot with peppercorns that fell from sacks. Nobody has proven it.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Bak kut teh

name: Belacan
tagline: The stink that makes the sambal.
story: Belacan is fermented shrimp paste, the base of sambal belacan. Toasted, it gives off a smell that newcomers often find too much, which is why cooks wrap it in foil first.
Colonial-era newspapers wrote about it mostly because of the smell. One British writer compared it to fine caviar but warned the smell was 'decidedly objectionable'.

sources.title: BiblioAsia: Of belacan and curry puffs

everyday.text: Sambal, of chilli, shrimp paste, lime, sugar and salt, is listed in Singapore's intangible cultural heritage inventory.

src.title: Roots: Making and use of sambal

name: Coconut milk
tagline: What makes nasi lemak 'lemak'.
story: Lemak means rich or creamy in Malay, and nasi lemak gets its name from rice cooked in santan, coconut milk, with pandan leaves for fragrance. Lemongrass, ginger or fenugreek can go in too.
Santan is squeezed from freshly grated coconut. It's traditionally steamed into the rice, because over a hot fire coconut milk burns easily.

everyday.text: Nasi lemak is traditionally wrapped in banana leaf.

src.title: Wikipedia: Nasi lemak

name: Axe Brand oil
tagline: The green bottle in every Singapore bag.
story: In 1928 Leung Yun Chee, newly arrived from Shunde in China, met a German physician in Singapore, Dr Schmeidler, who gave him a formula for a medicated oil of menthol, camphor and eucalyptus. He founded Leung Kai Fook Medical Company to sell it and chose the axe as his logo.
In Malay it's minyak angin cap kapak. It's still made in Singapore by the same family and sold in more than 50 countries.

sources.title: Roots: Axe brand medicated oil advertisement tray
Mothership: Axe Brand founder's eldest son

everyday.text: The National Heritage Board holds a 1960s–70s Axe Brand advertising tray in its collection.

src.title: Roots: Axe brand medicated oil advertisement tray

name: Fogging
tagline: The white cloud that rolls through the estate.
story: In dengue clusters, workers carry machines that heat insecticide into a thick white fog and walk it through drains and void decks. The fog has long used diesel as its carrier, which gives it its heavy, oily smell; newer water-based fogs are almost odourless.
NEA says fogging only kills the adult mosquitoes it reaches and should be used sparingly, alongside clearing the stagnant water where they breed.

sources.title: NEA: Fogging should be used judiciously
Wild Singapore News: Routine fogging harmful to health

everyday.text: In 2013, Singapore's worst dengue epidemic, more than 22,000 people were infected.

src.title: Wild Singapore News: Fight against dengue needs newer methods

name: Bak kwa
tagline: Charcoal smoke and caramelised pork, every New Year.
story: Bak kwa, 'dried meat' in Hokkien, is thin sheets of sweet, savoury pork. Here it took on a local twist: after air-drying, it's grilled over charcoal, which gives it its smoky smell.
Demand peaks before Chinese New Year, when the queues outside famous shops in Chinatown can run for hours.

everyday.text: In 2007, Bloomberg's Singapore office launched a tongue-in-cheek 'Bak Kwa Index' tracking New Year prices at four shops.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Bak kwa

name: Rubber latex
tagline: The sap that built Malaya's fortunes.
story: In 1877, 22 rubber seedlings arrived from Sri Lanka; 12 were planted at the Singapore Botanic Gardens. Henry Ridley, the Gardens' first director from 1888, refined a herring-bone tapping method that collects latex for decades without killing the tree.
He pushed planters so hard they called him 'Mad Ridley'. Rubber went on to become Malaya's great plantation crop.

sources.title: Singapore Botanic Gardens: Ridley and the rubber industry

name: Satay smoke
tagline: The smell of Boon Tat Street at 7pm.
story: Up to the late 1970s, the travelling satay man walked Singapore's streets with a portable charcoal grill. Many later settled into permanent stalls, most famously the Satay Club by the Esplanade.
Today the smoke rolls out every evening on Boon Tat Street beside Lau Pa Sat, which closes to traffic so the satay stalls can set up.

everyday.text: In 2007, Lau Pa Sat made the world's longest satay for the Guinness record: 140 m, with 150 kg of chicken.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Satay

name: Milo
tagline: The smell of sports day and the green van.
story: Milo is chocolate and malt powder, and for generations of Singaporeans it smells of school sports days, when the green Milo van handed out cups of cold Milo.
Milo Dinosaur, iced Milo with a heap of extra powder on top, is thought to have been named in Singapore's Indian Muslim eateries in the mid-1990s.

sources.title: IIAS: Milo Dinosaur, a Southeast Asian national beverage
National Museum: A history of the Milo Dinosaur

everyday.text: A&A Restaurant on Sembawang Road, now Teh Tarik Muslim Restaurant, claims to have invented Milo Dinosaur.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Teh tarik

name: Pineapple
tagline: Prosperity, baked into a tart.
story: In Hokkien, pineapple is ong lai, which sounds like 'fortune comes'. So pineapple turns up in Chinese New Year snacks and decorations.
The pineapple tart, buttery pastry with pineapple jam, was mainly made in Peranakan Chinese homes before it became the New Year staple it is now.

sources.title: NLB Infopedia: Chinese New Year food
Singapore Chinese Cultural Centre: CNY snacks

name: Chinese herbs
tagline: Six hundred drawers of roots and bark.
story: Step into a traditional medical hall and the smell of dried roots, bark and herbs hits first. A hall can hold over 600 herbs in its drawers, combined into thousands of brews.
Eu Yan Sang opened its first Singapore hall in 1910 at South Bridge Road. Its staff also helped migrants who couldn't read to write letters and send money home.

sources.title: Singapore Heritage Festival: Life in a traditional medical hall
Roots: Street Corner Heritage Galleries, Chinatown

everyday.text: Dang gui and other herbs give the dark Hokkien-style bak kut teh its medicinal smell.

src.title: Johor Kaki: Herbal bak kut teh

name: Laksa leaf
tagline: The sharp green herb on top of the bowl.
story: Daun kesum, or simply 'laksa leaf', is Vietnamese coriander: a peppery, citrusy herb scattered over laksa. Laksa itself is credited to the Peranakan Chinese.
Katong laksa, from the Peranakan neighbourhood of Katong, is Singapore's own version: coconut gravy, short-cut noodles you eat with just a spoon, and a heap of chopped laksa leaf.

everyday.text: Katong became known for laksa through two hugely popular 1960s stalls, Marine Parade Laksa and Roxy Laksa.

src.title: Carry It Like Harry: Singapore Katong laksa

name: Saffron
tagline: The gold threads in a pot of nasi briyani.
story: Saffron, steeped in warm milk, is what tints and scents the rice in nasi briyani. Islamic Restaurant on North Bridge Road has served briyani since 1921, when M. Abdul Rahiman, chef to the wealthy Arab Alsagoff family, opened it.
Its rice and meat are layered in a giant pot, and its diners have included Singapore's first president, Yusof Ishak.

sources.title: The Straits Times: Violet Oon's quest for the best briyani

everyday.text: Briyani in Singapore usually comes with achar, a pickle of cucumber, onion, chilli and pineapple.

src.title: SG101: Nasi briyani in Singapore

name: Turmeric & curry powder
tagline: Freshly ground in Little India.
story: Little India's spice shops sell turmeric, cumin, coriander seed and nutmeg by the scoop, and a few still grind their own blends. Thandapani Co, started by Sanmugam in the 1960s, bought over Valli Flour Mills in the 1970s so it could grind spices to its own recipes.

sources.title: Roots: Street Corner Heritage Galleries, Little India

everyday.text: At Tekka Centre, the spice-grinding machinery was originally brought in from India.

src.title: Wikipedia: Little India, Singapore

name: Bunga tanjung
tagline: Tiny star flowers that perfume the night.
story: The tanjong tree's small cream flowers open at twilight, grow more fragrant through the night, and drop by morning. It's commonly planted along roads in Singapore's housing estates.
A few are Heritage Trees, including one on Lorong Ah Soo in Hougang and one on Sentosa.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Mimusops elengi

lore.text: In Malay folklore the bunga tanjung often stands for a lost lover, and its flowers are said to chase away evil spirits.

src.title: Tutu Dutta: In search of the sundal tree

name: Gelam
tagline: The tree that gave Kampong Gelam its name.
story: Kampong Gelam is named after the gelam tree, Melaleuca cajuputi, a native tree with papery bark and tiny cream flowers that once grew in the area.
Oil from its leaves, cajuput oil, has a fresh, medicinal smell. It went into traditional Malay remedies made and sold in Kampong Gelam, and it's one of the oils in Tiger Balm.

sources.title: NParks: HortPark Streets of Singapore walk

name: Benzoin
tagline: Sweet resin smoke, traded through Singapore.
story: Kemenyan is benzoin, a resin tapped from Styrax trees in Sumatra. Burned, it gives a sweet, vanilla-like smoke used in incense across the Middle East, India and Asia.
For decades most of Sumatra's raw benzoin was shipped to Singapore, pressed into blocks here and re-exported to the Middle East, Africa, India and the rest of Asia.

sources.title: CIFOR: Harum madu dan dupa kemenyan

lore.text: In Java, kemenyan is still burned in rituals connected with death and spirits.

src.title: PROSEA: Styrax (benzoin)

name: Chrysanthemum
tagline: The cooling tea for a 'heaty' day.
story: Dried chrysanthemum flowers brewed into a pale golden tea are a classic liang cha, or cooling drink, for when the body feels 'heaty'. You'll find them in medical halls and supermarkets, and as boxed drinks.
Eu Yan Sang's Five Flower Tea blends chrysanthemum with honeysuckle, cotton tree flower, pagoda tree flower and frangipani.

sources.title: Eu Yan Sang: Five Flower Tea
My Wok Life: Chrysanthemum ginger tea

name: Hibiscus
tagline: The 'shoe flower' that became a national symbol next door.
story: Bunga raya, the 'grand' or 'celebratory' flower, was named Malaysia's national flower in 1960. In Malay and Indonesian it's also bunga sepatu, the shoe flower, because its petals were used to make black shoe polish.
The juice of its petals was used by Chinese and Indian communities to darken hair and eyebrows.

lore.text: Malays once used the flowers in exorcism rituals during epidemics.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Hibiscus

name: Cardamom
tagline: The green pod in a glass of teh masala.
story: Masala tea, or masala chai, comes from the Indian subcontinent: milk tea simmered with spices such as cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and ginger. In Singapore you'll find it at Indian restaurants and drink stalls as teh masala.
Every household has its own blend of spices for it.

sources.title: Roots: Making and sharing of tea

everyday.text: Teh masala sits on the menu next to teh tarik and teh halia at Indian Muslim drink stalls like Bhai Sarbat.

src.title: Roots: Bhai Sarbat

name: Chinese tea
tagline: Poured for the elders at a Chinese wedding.
story: Tea is teh in Malay, cha in Chinese and theneer in Tamil, and making and sharing it is listed in Singapore's intangible cultural heritage inventory.
At a traditional Chinese wedding, the couple serve tea to their elders as a sign of respect, starting at the groom's home.

sources.title: Roots: Making and sharing of tea

everyday.text: Bak kut teh is traditionally paired with a pot of Chinese tea.

src.title: Roots: Making and sharing of tea

name: Camphor
tagline: A forest giant that once supplied the world's camphor.
story: Kapur, Dryobalanops aromatica, is a towering rainforest tree with fragrant resin; it was an important source of natural camphor, the cooling, medicinal smell also found in Tiger Balm and Axe oil.
Three kapur trees are Heritage Trees in Singapore. Those at the Botanic Gardens grew from seeds the botanist E.J.H. Corner collected on Malaya's east coast; one was planted on 15 January 1940.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Dryobalanops aromatica

lore.text: Kapur shows 'crown shyness': the tops of neighbouring trees stop just short of touching, leaving channels of sky between them.

src.title: Wikipedia: Dryobalanops aromatica

name: Ketupat leaf
tagline: Rice boiled in a woven coconut-leaf diamond.
story: Ketupat is rice packed into a pouch woven from young coconut leaves and boiled until it sets. About a week before Hari Raya, young coconut leaves appear at markets so families can weave their own.

In Singapore it's served at Hari Raya Puasa, Hari Raya Haji and Malay weddings, and woven ketupat hang as festive decorations too. Weaving ketupat is listed in Singapore's intangible cultural heritage inventory.

lore.text: The Malay Muslim community traditionally eats ketupat by cutting it in half, not by peeling away the leaves.

src.title: Roots: Weaving ketupat

name: Ghee & sesame oil
tagline: The smell of a Deepavali morning.
story: Deepavali means 'a row of lights'. Homes are lit with small clay oil lamps, and on the morning itself many Hindus wake early for an oil bath, often with gingelly (sesame) oil.
The festival sweets are rich in ghee: mithai, adhirasam made with jaggery, and nei urundai, literally 'ghee balls'.

name: Rain on hot ground
tagline: The smell right before the afternoon thunderstorm.
story: Petrichor is the earthy smell when rain hits dry ground: oils from plants and geosmin from soil bacteria, thrown into the air by the first drops. Before a storm, lightning adds a sharp, clean smell of ozone.
In Singapore, the monsoon months bring regular late-morning and afternoon thundery showers. Epilogue's Senator, I'm Singaporean builds its base around this smell of wet soil after sudden rain.

sources.title: Time Out Singapore: NEA weather advisory

name: Mangrove mud
tagline: Salt, mud and leaf litter at low tide.
story: Mangroves grow in the tidal mud between land and sea, and give off the sulphurous, salty smell of low tide. Singapore has more than 30 mangrove species; the largest mainland mangrove, 130 hectares, is at Sungei Buloh.
Sungei Buloh was nearly cleared for an agrotech park until birdwatchers proposed saving it in 1986. It opened as a nature park in 1993 and became a nature reserve in 2002.

sources.title: NLB Infopedia: Sungei Buloh Wetland Reserve
Mothership: Sungei Buloh almost became an agrotech park
NParks Buzz: Trees of the mangroves

everyday.text: The sulphur smell comes from bacteria breaking things down in the airless mud.

src.title: Wild Shores of Singapore: White mud at Pasir Ris

lore.text: Places once named after mangroves, like Kampong Sungei Attap and Sungei Bakau Rungkup in Jurong, no longer exist.

src.title: BiblioAsia: Mangroves, a tale of survival

name: Galangal
tagline: The piney root in a pot of Hari Raya rendang.
story: Lengkuas, or blue ginger, is a sharper, piney cousin of ginger. It's pounded with chilli, lemongrass, garlic, shallot, kaffir lime leaves and turmeric into the paste for rendang, meat stewed slowly in coconut milk.
Rendang comes from the Minangkabau of West Sumatra. In Singapore it's a celebratory dish for Hari Raya and Malay weddings.

lore.text: In the old days, rendang was wrapped in plantain or banana leaves to carry on long journeys.

src.title: NLB Infopedia: Rendang

name: Curry leaf
tagline: Sizzling in the oil before the fish head goes in.
story: Curry leaves are a backbone of South Indian cooking, fried in oil at the start of a curry. They're a key smell in fish head curry, a dish born in Singapore.

In 1949, Marian Jacob Gomez, a Malayali from Kerala, opened a restaurant on Sophia Road and started cooking whole fish heads in his curry for his Chinese customers, who prized the head. It's listed in Singapore's intangible cultural heritage inventory.

everyday.text: You can see a curry tree growing in the Spice Garden at Fort Canning Park.

src.title: NParks: Fort Canning Spice Garden trail

name: Tamarind
tagline: The sour in asam pedas.
story: Tamarind pulp is asam, the sour backbone of asam pedas, Peranakan gerang asam and Indian fish curries. In Malay the tree is asam jawa.
Tamarind trees line several Singapore streets, and three are Heritage Trees, including one in the grounds of the Istana.

everyday.text: The pulp is also eaten on its own as a sweet-sour preserved snack, and it goes into Worcestershire sauce.

src.title: NParks Heritage Tree HT 2001-28

lore.text: There's a huge asam tree at the Pulau Ubin jetty, beside the shops.

src.title: Wild Shores of Singapore: Asam tree at Changi Creek

name: Honeysuckle
tagline: The 'gold and silver flower' of cooling tea.
story: In Chinese medicine, Japanese honeysuckle is jin yin hua, 'gold and silver flower', because its blooms open white and turn yellow. Dried, it's brewed into cooling teas for a heaty sore throat.
It's one of the five flowers in the Five Flower Tea sold at Eu Yan Sang, alongside chrysanthemum and frangipani.

sources.title: PULSE TCM: Honeysuckle and chrysanthemum tea
Eu Yan Sang: Five Flower Tea

name: Orange blossom water
tagline: Sprinkled on the flowers of a Malay wedding.
story: At a Malay wedding, guests are given bunga rampai: shredded pandan with bunga setaman, flowers scented with rosewater or orange blossom water.
Elders bless the couple on the dais by sprinkling rosewater and flower potpourri over them.

name: Cinnamon
tagline: 'Sweet wood', in bak kut teh and teh masala.
story: In Malay cinnamon is kayu manis, 'sweet wood'. It's simmered in Hokkien-style bak kut teh with star anise and cloves, and in masala tea with cardamom and ginger.
A cinnamon tree grows in the Spice Garden at Fort Canning, on the site of Raffles' first botanic garden.

sources.title: Roots: Making and sharing of tea
NParks: Fort Canning Spice Garden trail

name: Mangosteen
tagline: The 'cooling' queen eaten after the king.
story: Mangosteen, manggis in Malay, is the queen to durian's king: a purple rind around soft, white, sweet-sour segments.

NParks notes that some Chinese eat the two together, believing durian is 'heaty' and mangosteen 'cooling'. Doctors say there's no evidence for it; the two simply ripen in the same season, around June to August.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Garcinia mangostana

lore.text: Some people pour water into an empty durian husk and drink it to 'cool down' after a durian feast.

src.title: Singapore for Less: Durians and mangosteens

name: Chempedak
tagline: Jackfruit's pungent cousin, best fried.
story: Chempedak is a cousin of jackfruit with a pungent smell often compared to durian. Inside are sweet, sticky golden pods around large seeds.
The pods are dipped in batter and deep-fried into fritters, sold at roadside stalls across the region.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Artocarpus integer

everyday.text: There's a chempedak Heritage Tree on Sentosa.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Artocarpus integer

name: Holy basil
tagline: The sacred basil grown in temple courtyards.
story: Tulsi, holy basil, is sacred to Hindus and a symbol of loyalty and devotion. It's often planted in courtyards and temple gardens, and its fragrant leaves are used in prayers.
Lord Krishna is said to wear a garland of tulsi leaves and flowers, and its woody stems are carved into prayer beads.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Ocimum tenuiflorum

lore.text: Some believe water should not be offered to the plant during a lunar eclipse.

src.title: NParks Buzz: Basil, the king of herbs

name: Dried mandarin peel
tagline: Peel that gets more precious every year.
story: Chenpi, 'aged peel', is sun-dried mandarin peel kept for years. It turns darker and sweeter with age; the finest grade is 10 years old or more, and old peel sells for luxury prices.
A few pieces scent Cantonese red bean soup. It's also steeped into teas at medical halls.

lore.text: Families keep red chenpi as heirlooms and gift it to brides.

src.title: Johor Kaki: Chenpi worth more than gold

name: Joss paper
tagline: Burning gold paper in the metal bins.
story: Joss paper, spirit money and paper replicas of houses, cars and clothes are burned for ancestors and wandering spirits, above all during the seventh lunar month and Qingming.
Town councils put out metal burning bins in housing estates, and temples have large furnaces for mass prayer.

sources.title: Roots: Zhong Yuan Jie (Hungry Ghost Festival)
Ang Mo Kio Town Council: Burning joss paper
The HomeGround Asia: Hungry Ghost Festival explained

everyday.text: Some companies burn paper offerings worth over S$1,000 in Chinatown's back lanes during the festival.

src.title: Religion News Service: Hungry Ghost Month in Singapore

name: Ironwood flower
tagline: The tree the next Buddha will sit under.
story: Mesua ferrea, penaga lilin in Malay, bears large, very fragrant flowers of four white waxy petals around a golden ball of stamens. Its wood is so dense that it sinks in water even when dry.
Buddhists believe the next Buddha, Maitreya, will reach enlightenment under this tree. Its flowers are given as temple offerings, and its seed oil once lit Buddhist temple lamps.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Mesua ferrea

lore.text: Maitreya is traditionally shown holding a Mesua ferrea flower.

src.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Mesua ferrea

name: Banana shrub
tagline: A magnolia that smells like fruity chewing gum.
story: Magnolia figo, called chempaka ambon or banana shrub, has small creamy flowers wrapped in furry brown buds. NParks describes the scent as ripe honeydew, bananas or fruity chewing gum, strongest towards evening.
In Chinese it's 含笑花, han xiao hua: the 'holding a smile' flower.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Magnolia figo

name: Water gardenia
tagline: A native gardenia lost from the wild.
story: Gardenia tubifera is a native tree of swamp forests and estuaries, with fragrant flowers that open cream and turn orange-yellow the next day. In Singapore it's listed as presumed nationally extinct in the wild.
It survives here in cultivation; NParks lists it as suitable for roadsides, parks and fragrant gardens.

sources.title: NParks Flora & Fauna Web: Gardenia tubifera
